title: Did AI Just Make an Exercise Pill?
description: The biotechnology company Enveda just announced what could be a first-of-its-kind exercise pill. I say “ first-of-its-kind ” not just because of its biological effects, but because of how it was discovered. Enveda, a company with which I have no conflicts of interest, has the motto, “Life is smart, let’s learn from it.” And they’re now using AI to help sort through the library of natural molecules found in our bodies and those of other organisms to try to develop metabolic medicines. And they might have just had a major breakthrough, with positive results from a Phase 1 trial for a compound called ENV-308, which is being termed: “The first pill designed from the chemistry of exercise.” The story here is beautiful, but to really understand it, we need to start with a problem. How We Discover Drugs Today It’s easiest to describe the problem by telling you how we discover drugs right now. We first identify a target, like a receptor or a desired biomarker change, and then try to figure out how to impact that target. For example, when it comes to heart health, one target medicine chose to focus on was cholesterol. So, we went looking for things that inhibit cholesterol synthesis. Eventually, we came to statins. You could say something similar about the discovery of blood pressure medications, and so on. This new approach flips the script. It looks at desirable physiological states, the buffet of natural compounds with which they’re associated, and then figures out what in that complex biological soup is actually relevant. Take exercise. When you exercise, thousands of molecules change in your blood.

title: How To Pick Your Protein (MD PhD Explains)
description: If you spend a decent amount of time in the corners of nutrition social media, you’ll hear a multitude of opinions about how to pick your protein. What’s the real difference between grass-fed and grass-and-grain-fed beef? Wild salmon versus farmed salmon? What about pollutants? Pasture-raised eggs versus free-range eggs versus organic eggs? And are sardines really loaded with heavy metals? Today, my goal is simple: to tell you what I look for, what I care about, and how I make my choices in the grocery store. Think of this letter as a practical reference guide. Like some good biltong, it’s going to be a little drier than our usual StayCurious Metabolism fare, but I hope it serves as a useful resource for those of you who want to make informed decisions when it comes to picking your protein. And I apologize in advance, but there will be no discussion of tofu. Premium subscribers get full access to my deep dives into cutting-edge metabolic research for less than $1/letter, 3 per week. You’ll always walk away with at least one new insight about metabolic health. Today’s letter is a special for StayCurious Metabolism premium members. We’ll dive specifically into: Beef : what actually matters… and what doesn’t. Eggs and their many confusing labels , along with some important nuances that most people never discuss. Poultry , including the nuances of methionine and glycine ratios. Seafood , from heavy metals and contaminants to my new favorite canned item (not sardines). Dairy , including fermented dairy products and the casein debate. Along the way, I’ll share some fun facts, personal favorites, and practical takeaways.

title: I Compared Every Popular Caffeine Source – Here's What I Learned
description: If I gave you 100 mg of caffeine… and then I gave you another 100 mg of caffeine, and then another... you’d think they’d feel the same, right? But they don’t. Coffee can make some people laser-focused and productive. Green tea can feel calm and almost meditative. Yerba mate has developed a cult following among entrepreneurs who swear it gives them energy without the crash. And somehow, dark chocolate contains caffeine too—yet nobody eats a square of chocolate and feels like they just drank an espresso. So, what’s going on? It turns out that the source of your caffeine matters at much, or more, than amount of caffeine itself. So the question is: Why do different caffeinated drinks feel so different if they’re all delivering the same drug? The Caffeine Entourage Let’s start with the concept that ties it all together. In pharmacology, there’s a concept sometimes called the “entourage effect” — the idea that a bioactive compound doesn’t act in isolation. Its effects are shaped by the other molecules traveling alongside it. Think of caffeine as a lead singer. Talented, yes. But the final product depends entirely on the band behind them. The “band members” are molecules like L-theanine, theobromine, theophylline, chlorogenic acids, catechins, and tannins. Each caffeine source packages a unique combination of these compounds — the “ entourage ” — and that combination determines the whole experience. So, if I give you 100 mg of caffeine from different sources, you won’t have the same experience. And, once you understand the underlying biology, you can start matching your caffeine source to your goal.
